# The Library of Unfinished Things

The first item was a blue mitten with no thumb.

It arrived in a paper bag between two returned novels and a notice about overdue fines. The mitten had been knitted from thick wool, the color of a winter sky just before snow. A loop of yarn hung where the thumb should have been. Inside the bag was a note written on the back of a grocery receipt: *I don’t know if you can use this. I couldn’t throw it away.*

At the time, the library accepted books, magazines, and, once, a box of slightly damp maps. We had no policy for mittens. I set it on my desk while I decided what to do.

That afternoon, a man came in carrying a cardboard tube. He asked if we still had the table by the window, the one where people sometimes worked on puzzles. I told him we did. He withdrew a drawing from the tube and unrolled it carefully.

It showed a greenhouse, measured and labeled in neat pencil. Along one edge, he had sketched shelves for seedlings. Along another were two chairs and a small table. The drawing stopped halfway through the roof.

“My wife made this,” he said. “She was going to build it behind our house.”

I waited. People brought all kinds of things to the library when they needed a place to start talking.

“She got sick,” he said. “Now I’m selling the house. I thought someone might like the plan.”

I looked at the greenhouse, at its unfinished roof and its two chairs. I thought of the mitten on my desk.

“Would you let me keep it for a little while?” I asked.

By closing time, both objects were on the puzzle table. I made two cards from the blank backs of old catalog slips. On the first I wrote, *Blue mitten. Maker unknown.* On the second: *Greenhouse plan. Donated by Mr. Alvarez.* I left enough room below each description for more information, if anyone had it.

The next morning, someone had added a third thing: a letter in an envelope addressed only to “My brother.” It was unsigned and ended after three sentences. The writer had described seeing a dog on the bus that looked just like one they had loved as children. Nothing explained why the letter had never been sent. It might have been written the day before, or twenty years earlier.

I should have taken the letter to the lost-and-found drawer. Instead, I gave it a card.

Our library occupied the ground floor of a former post office. It had high windows, stone floors, and a heating system that clanked whenever the temperature dropped. We had enough room for the collection only because the reference shelves had grown smaller over the years. On quiet afternoons, sunlight reached across the empty shelves and stopped at the puzzle table.

That was where the unfinished things gathered. Within a month there was a model airplane missing one wing, a cookbook with handwritten recipes through page eleven, and a quilt square embroidered with twelve tiny strawberries. Someone left a cassette tape labeled *Dad’s stories* with no indication of what was on it. A child deposited a clay horse with three legs and a note that said, *I got tired but I still like him.*

We began calling the table the Library of Unfinished Things. No one officially approved the name. There was no budget line or committee. People came in, looked around, and sometimes brought something on their next visit.

My colleague Priya was less enchanted than I was. She had worked at the library for twenty-three years and knew exactly how quickly a charming idea could become a storage problem.

“Where does it end?” she asked when a woman arrived with the pieces of a half-built rocking chair.

“At the edge of the table,” I said.

“I hope the chair understands that.”

Priya helped the woman carry the pieces inside. Then she found a box so nobody would trip over the curved runners. This was typical of Priya: she saw the problem clearly and helped anyway.

Soon we needed rules. Nothing sharp, perishable, or too large for one person to carry. Donors could stay anonymous. They could take their things back. Other people could look, but they could not work on anything without permission. The last rule mattered. Several visitors had offered to finish the mitten, and I could not shake the feeling that its maker might return one day wanting to find it just as they had left it.

For a while, I thought the point of the table was to give people somewhere to put things they no longer wanted at home. Then I began to notice how long visitors stayed. Mr. Alvarez came twice a week to sit near the greenhouse plan and read the newspaper. A woman who donated an unfinished song brought headphones so she could listen to the cassette player beside it. She never played past the point where her voice stopped.

The clay horse became a favorite among the children who came in after school. They argued over whether it was running or standing still. One boy thought it must be leaning against something outside the frame. His friend pointed out that a horse with three legs could simply be a horse with three legs. They made room for it on the table after every Saturday craft session.

At home, I had my own collection, though I kept it out of sight. There was a scarf I had begun during a winter of long hospital visits, a packet of seeds bought for a garden I never dug, and an email to my father saved in drafts. The email asked him how he had made the soup he cooked whenever someone was ill. It was a plain question, but I kept rewriting it. By the time I had a version I liked, he had died.

I had never mentioned the email at work. In the library, I was good at writing labels for other people’s things.

In late October, the city announced that the post office building needed electrical repairs. The library would close for six weeks while contractors opened walls and replaced wiring. We had ten days to box the books and move the most-used services to two rooms in the community center. There would be no space there for the puzzle table.

I told the donors their objects would be stored safely until we reopened. Most accepted this without concern. The woman with the rocking chair took its pieces home, saying she needed the box for a move. Mr. Alvarez asked if he might keep the greenhouse plan during the closure.

“Of course,” I said.

He rolled it up slowly. “I’ve been wondering about the roof,” he said. “I think she meant for it to collect rainwater. She talked about barrels all the time.”

He pointed to a short pencil line I had taken for part of a shelf. Once he said it, I could see the gutter it might have become.

The following day, the school caretaker came in to examine the model airplane. He knew how to build the missing wing, he said, if the owner wanted help. A woman who had read the anonymous letter asked whether we could leave paper beside it, so people could write letters of their own. Priya found a packet of stationery in a supply cupboard. By the end of the week, the envelope had a small stack of companions, all addressed, none sealed.

As I packed the table, I realized how much of the collection I knew through other people’s attention. I knew where the cookbook fell open because visitors searched it for the recipe called “Sunday beans.” I knew that a chip on the clay horse’s ear had been there from the start because one of the children checked it every visit. Each person had noticed something I might have missed.

On our final afternoon, the mitten’s maker came back.

She was a young woman in a yellow raincoat, carrying a stack of picture books. She stopped by the table, picked up the mitten, and smiled with the brief, startled expression of someone recognizing an old photograph.

“I left this,” she said.

“I’m glad you came in. We’re packing everything away for the building repairs.”

She turned the mitten over in her hands. “I was learning to knit when my daughter was a baby. She’s twelve now. I never figured out the thumb.”

“You can take it home.”

She looked at the dangling yarn. “I think I will. She might get a laugh out of it.”

She checked out the books, tucked the mitten into her coat pocket, and left. I had imagined a much sadder story for it. All I really knew was what she had written on the receipt: she couldn’t throw it away. Perhaps bringing it here had helped her see that she could carry it home.

The library closed. We spent November at the community center, sharing a hallway with a dance class and a weekly meeting about local roads. It was crowded and noisy, and people kept finding us. They returned books at a folding table. They asked when the post office building would reopen. A few asked after particular objects: the song, the horse, the greenhouse. I told them where each one was packed.

In December, the contractors finished. We carried boxes back across town and opened the doors on a cold Monday morning. The puzzle table was waiting by the window. I wiped the dust from it and brought the collection out of storage.

There was less to arrange than I expected. The mitten and greenhouse plan were gone, along with the rocking chair. The other things looked smaller after their time in boxes. I set out the clay horse, the quilt square, the airplane, the cookbook, the song, and the letters. Priya found our old catalog cards and laid them beside the objects.

For several days, nothing new arrived. Then someone brought in a wooden birdhouse with its roof unattached. The maker had drilled an entrance hole too small for the birds he hoped would use it and wanted to know whether it could be widened. I knew almost nothing about birdhouses, so I wrote his question on a card. By the following week, three people had left suggestions, and one had offered to lend him a drill.

Mr. Alvarez returned in January carrying the greenhouse plan. He had drawn in the rest of the roof himself. Above it, on a separate sheet, he had made a list of questions for anyone who had built one before: how much ventilation it would need, whether the chairs were too close to the planting beds, what kind of barrel would survive the winter.

“I’m not building it at the old house,” he told me. “My sister has a place with a better yard.”

I cleared a space for both sheets. Soon a gardener who used the library computers began leaving notes in the margins, always in green pencil so Mr. Alvarez could distinguish her additions from his wife’s drawing. They discussed hinges and tomatoes without ever arriving at the same time. In March, he left a photograph of a bare patch of ground behind his sister’s house. Two chairs sat there in the sunlight.

The model airplane went home with its owner and returned a month later with a new wing, made with the caretaker’s help. It was a little heavier than the other one. The owner brought a photograph of the plane in flight, so we could see that it flew well enough. The cookbook remained at page eleven, though three visitors copied out the Sunday beans recipe and one returned to say she had made it for her family. The letter to a brother was never claimed. It stayed in its envelope while people read the letters beside it and sometimes added another.

One evening, after we closed, I opened a new document on a library computer and typed out the question I had meant to send my father. Then I wrote down everything I remembered about his soup: how the kitchen window clouded while it simmered, how he cut the carrots into thick pieces, how he tasted it from a spoon and usually added more salt. I could picture the pot but not all the ingredients. I printed the page anyway.

The next morning I put it on the table with a card that read, *Soup recipe, reconstructed from memory. Suggestions welcome.* Priya read it before opening the doors.

“Needs celery,” she said, taking a pencil from behind her ear.

“Maybe,” I said.

“I’d bet on it.”

She wrote *celery?* in the margin, and I wrote her name beside it. Over the next few weeks, other people added garlic, barley, lemon, and an argument about whether the carrots should go in first or last. I tried several versions at home. None tasted exactly like my father’s, though one came close enough that I sat down with my bowl and remembered a winter evening when he had set the pot between us on the table.

Spring brought more donations. We accepted some, sent others to places better suited to them, and made room when we could. The birdhouse maker came back for his card after widening the hole. The yellow raincoat appeared one rainy Saturday; its owner showed me a picture of her daughter wearing the blue mitten on one hand and a red glove on the other. The daughter had asked to keep the loose loop of yarn.

At the end of each day, I straightened the cards and checked that the small things had not drifted too close to the table’s edge. Sometimes I found a new note. Sometimes an object was gone because its owner had taken it home. I liked both kinds of change. They gave me something to tell Priya when she returned from locking the front doors, and something to wonder about when I switched off the lamps.

The post office windows faced west. In the last light, the quilt’s strawberries glowed against the pale cloth, and the clay horse cast a long, three-legged shadow. I would make one final circuit of the room, then leave everything where it was. The table had become part of the library’s evening quiet: books on their shelves, chairs pushed in, a few unfinished things waiting by the window for whoever came through the doors tomorrow.
